extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and students/scholars of political theory and comparative history (readers of Popular Science Monthly)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical essay on the origins, structure, and sustaining forces of political authority across societies, tracing primitive triune agencies, the role of public sentiment (present and ancestral), effects of war and conquest, and the constraints on rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triune political structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Early political organization shows 'vague outlines of a triune political structure' composed of (1) the assembled people, (2) a body of chosen chiefs or magistrates, and (3) a controlling head or chief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by practices such as the Icelandic Al-thing and Var-things, the Swiss cantonal yearly meetings, and hints in the Wittenagemot; ratios among the three components vary by society and over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of public assembly and vocal approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Primitive political decision-making often took place in public assemblies where speakers influenced by persuasion and approval/disapproval (shouts, clashing spears) determined outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Icelandic assemblies where 'the judges sat, the people standing on the outside' and English Wittenagemot indications that kings were 'chosen by all folk' with the people's approval expressed by shouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergence of individual predominance via recognized superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals acquire predominant influence through recognized superiority in sagacity, skill, strength, or perceived supernatural character, sometimes becoming hereditary leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unusual sagacity or strength regarded as supernatural can grant one member influence that is transmitted to successors; this helps explain the early appearance of a controlling head.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labor shapes power relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Division of labor (e.g., exclusivity of warrior roles) can change the balance among the triune components, enabling some parts to override others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If some are exclusively warriors while others handle different tasks, the warrior/leader components gain ability to dominate the third (mass) component; examples discussed in primitive tribes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of passive/non-political classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Political evolution often creates a passive class (initially women, then slaves/dependents) excluded from deliberation, altering the relation of governing elements to the whole community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As political structures evolve, some components shrink or disappear and passive classes become excluded from decision-making, impacting the ratios of political power.

rubrics_metrics.name: War promotes subordination and centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful warfare tends to establish subordination, increase the controlling power of dominant few, and favor obedience to a single head, thereby centralizing political authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groups with greater subordination often survive over less subordinated ones; chronic warfare selects for prompt, consistent action and obedience—leading to stronger heads and more centralized rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political types derived from primitive components' relative development
rubrics_metrics.description: Despotism, oligarchy, and democracy are to be regarded as types in which one of the original triune components has greatly developed at the expense of the other two; mixed types reflect intermediate proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political forms should be classified according to which original component predominates; historical shifts in proportions explain transitions among forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary source of political power: aggregate public feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate source of political power is the feeling of the community—both present public opinion and, more largely, the organized sentiments inherited from past generations—rather than intrinsic government power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: just as water's destructive power comes from wind driven by solar heating, government power is instrumental, deriving from broader social forces; evidence includes practices where public sentiment restrains rulers and enforces norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misattribution of power to visible agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a common tendency to associate power with visible agents (governments, rulers) instead of recognizing the inconspicuous social sources (collective feelings, traditions) that actually enable that power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tendency vitiates political conceptions; the essay stresses tracing power back through institutions to popular sentiment and ultimately to transmitted cultural forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control by inherited customs and ancestral sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Much political restraint and regulation arises from long-standing customs and the emotional attachment to ancestors' practices; these transmitted opinions often operate more strongly than current institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ritual mutilations, tattooing, and other imperative customs; Tupis' belief in destruction for departing from ancestors' customs; Juangs' resistance to change; Sumatra's 'adat' customs governing disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-institutional social enforcement mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: In societies lacking formal political control, social mechanisms—public disgrace, satirical singing-combat, banishment, admonition, fines, excommunication, and social taunting—enforce norms effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greenland singing-combat, Australian expulsion for theft, Columbian tribes' banishment, and social pressure on avengers illustrate how informal sanctions regulate behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited coercive authority of early chiefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Early or primitive chiefs often have little coercive power; their authority depends on popularity, personal service, and the degree to which they express the wills of others rather than impose their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Snake Indians where each is his own master; Chinook chiefs whose authority rests on service and popularity; Dakota chiefs unable to act for the tribe; Creek chiefs' authority limited by public disapproval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition from custom to written law constrains rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: As orally-preserved custom becomes codified in written law, the political head becomes more clearly an agent through whom ancestral feelings act and becomes more constrained by precedent and custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances: Madagascar where sovereign's word suffices only if no law/custom exists; East African 'ada' as limit to despot's power; Javan chiefs restrained by regard for character and custom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conquest distorts normal source of political power
rubrics_metrics.description: Societies formed by conquest often lack unified communal feeling; political heads in such contexts may derive power exclusively from the dominant group's feeling or rely on setting divergent masses against each other, making individual will a major factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conquest creates composite societies with alien components, so the usual derivation of political force from aggregate feeling is disrupted and rulers may exercise more unilateral will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraints and limits on autocratic power
rubrics_metrics.description: Even autocrats are constrained by accumulated institutions, religious sanctions, precedents, elite cooperation (military, ministers), and risk of removal (assassination or deposition); their power is strong only as influential classes support them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Egyptian dynasties retaining order despite despots; Amenhotep IV's religious reform later reversed; Roman emperors' dependence on soldiers; modern analogies to Russia where army desire affects the Czar.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'dead hand' of tradition as dominant causal force
rubrics_metrics.description: Established institutions and laws are consolidated products of past emotions and ideas; obedience and political action are largely produced by subordination of present sentiments to these inherited frameworks—the 'dead hand' controls living actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that the feeling of the community (past and present) is the sole source of political power in communities not under foreign domination; customs made sacred by tradition produce obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion's superiority over unenforced law/religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Where public opinion favors a practice (e.g., dueling), written law and religious sanctions often fail; an unwritten law enforced by strong opinion can be more peremptory than a written law without popular support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: persistence of dueling despite legal prohibitions; social codes (even about necktie color) enforced by opinion, and the tendency to honor 'debts of honor' over actual creditors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrence of triune divisions in modern associations
rubrics_metrics.description: The division into audience (mass), select influential group, and chosen head recurs in modern permanent associations (companies, societies, clubs), and the balance shifts depending on members' ability to cooperate or the distribution of ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Day-to-day public meetings, commercial companies, philanthropic societies, and clubs typically exhibit the three divisions; where wide distribution (e.g., railway shareholders) hinders cooperative action, select few can form an oligarchy.
